newsitem.title: ITALY: POLL - Italy recovery on way but employment lagging.
newsitem.headline: POLL - Italy recovery on way but employment lagging.

text.p: The Italian economy has touched bottom and is on the road to recovery, boosted by a less restrictive fiscal and monetary policy and by strong demand from abroad, a Reuters quarterly survey showed.
Analysts polled between June 30 and July 2 said the latest GDP and trade figures signal a recovery but they also said they were cautious about the chances of a rise in employment.

Forecasts carried out by 18 research departments point to an average 1.7 percent year-on-year increase in industrial production this year, rising to 3.4 percent in 1998. Output last year fell by 1.7 percent.

The consensus forecast for gross domestic product growth is 0.9 percent this year and two percent in 1998. This compares with the government's official target in a recently approved three-year economic programme of 1.2 percent this year and two percent next.
Analysts were more sceptical about the government's unemployment targets. The government is aiming to bring unemployment down to 11.7 percent in 1998 from a 12.0 percent target this year.
Economists polled by Reuters see unemployment at 12.3 percent at year-end, falling only slightly to 12 percent next year.
Paolo Casadio, economist at Credito Italiano, sounded an optimistic note about the future. "We will see a good GDP figure in the second quarter of 1997," he said.
Casadio is forecasting a one percent yewar-on-year rise in the second quarter and 0.9 percent for the whole of 1997.
"In the first quarter of 1997 the number of working days was at its lowest for three years, dragging down the GDP figure," said Casadio.
"This will be made up for in the coming months when the increase in working days together with a growth in stocks and the revival in foreign demand will fuel a revival in GDP," he added.

"In the first quarter of 1997 the number of working days reachest its lowest point in the last three years, lowering the the GDP figure. This will be made up for in the coming months when the increase in days worked and the buildup of stocks and the revival of foreign demand will fuel the revival in GDP," said Casadio.
Massimo Cilio of Sella Asset Management and Fabio Stolfa of Caboto sounded a more cautious note, saying that they did not expect concrete signs of recovery until late 1997 or early 1998.

"For the last five months now the leading indicators of our model had been positive. The Italian revival is lagging Germany's because monetary and fiscal policy hads been more restrictive than in other countries," said Cilio.
"An easing, even if only in relative terms, of these policies and the stimulus on the way from exports will make a recovery possible," said Sella Asset Management.
However, domestic demand and investments are expected to languish for many months to come.
"From September the reduction in interest rates will become very aggressive but the effects on domestic demand will not become apparent for nine to 12 months," said Fabio Stolfa at Caboto in Milan.
"The investment cycle will revive thanks to the stabilisation in prices, to the decline in interest rates and to innovation by comnpanies," said Cilio.
Credito Italiano is forecasting an annual average increase in gross fixed investments of 1.3 percent. "This trend is still too slow," said Credito's Casadio.
Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio said on Monday that the outlook for growth was uncertain because of the weakness of productive investments.
Fazio also warned that the tax burden was too high and the labour market was excessively regulated.

Unemployment is another sore point. "The number of jobless will start to decline when GDP increases by more than 2.5 percent, that is by more than the potential medium term growth rate," said Cilio at Sella Asset Management.
The government is forecasting 2.5 percent growth from 1999.
